claim: Drosophila mushroom body progenitors (neuroblasts) sequentially produce only three neuronal types: γ, then α'β', followed by αβ.
source: Temporal patterning of neural progenitors leads to the sequential production of diverse neurons. To understand how extrinsic cues influence intrinsic temporal programs, we studied Drosophila mushroom body progenitors (neuroblasts) that sequentially produce only three neuronal types: γ, then α'β', followed by αβ.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript showing the sequential production of these three neuronal types.

claim: Opposing gradients of two RNA-binding proteins Imp and Syp comprise the intrinsic temporal program in mushroom body neuroblasts.
source: Opposing gradients of two RNA-binding proteins Imp and Syp comprise the intrinsic temporal program.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing Imp and Syp expression patterns in neuroblasts throughout the manuscript.

claim: The activin ligand Myoglianin from glia regulates the temporal factor Imp in mushroom body neuroblasts.
source: We show that the activin ligand Myoglianin from glia regulates the temporal factor Imp in mushroom body neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that glial knockdown of Myoglianin affects Imp levels and α'β' neuron specification.

claim: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window.
source: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window, causing the loss of α'β' neurons, a decrease in αβ neurons, and a likely increase in γ neurons, without affecting the overall number of neurons produced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in Figure 2 showing higher Imp to Syp ratios in babo mutant neuroblasts.

claim: Loss of the activin receptor Baboon causes the loss of α'β' neurons.
source: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window, causing the loss of α'β' neurons, a decrease in αβ neurons, and a likely increase in γ neurons, without affecting the overall number of neurons produced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 showing absence of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones.

claim: Loss of the activin receptor Baboon causes a decrease in αβ neurons.
source: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window, causing the loss of α'β' neurons, a decrease in αβ neurons, and a likely increase in γ neurons, without affecting the overall number of neurons produced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figure 1K showing reduced αβ neuron numbers in babo mutant clones.

claim: Loss of the activin receptor Baboon likely causes an increase in γ neurons.
source: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window, causing the loss of α'β' neurons, a decrease in αβ neurons, and a likely increase in γ neurons, without affecting the overall number of neurons produced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1I showing a trend toward increased γ neuron numbers in babo mutant clones, though not statistically significant.

claim: Loss of the activin receptor Baboon does not affect the overall number of neurons produced.
source: Neuroblasts missing the activin receptor Baboon have a delayed intrinsic program as Imp is higher than normal during the α'β' temporal window, causing the loss of α'β' neurons, a decrease in αβ neurons, and a likely increase in γ neurons, without affecting the overall number of neurons produced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1H' showing no significant difference in clone sizes between wildtype and babo mutant clones.

claim: An extrinsic cue modifies an intrinsic temporal program to increase neuronal diversity.
source: Our results illustrate that an extrinsic cue modifies an intrinsic temporal program to increase neuronal diversity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the overall findings showing how activin signaling modulates the Imp temporal program.

claim: Individual radial glia progenitors in the vertebrate cortex sequentially give rise to neurons that occupy the different cortical layers in an inside-out manner.
source: For instance, individual radial glia progenitors in the vertebrate cortex sequentially give rise to neurons that occupy the different cortical layers in an inside-out manner (Gao et al., 2014; Llorca et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Projection neurons in the Drosophila antennal lobe are born in a stereotyped temporal order and innervate specific glomeruli.
source: For example, projection neurons in the antennal lobe are born in a stereotyped temporal order and innervate specific glomeruli (Jefferis et al., 2001; Kao et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Young cortical progenitors placed in an old host environment alter their output to match the host environment and produce upper-layer neurons.
source: Indeed, classic heterochronic transplantation experiments demonstrated that young cortical progenitors placed in an old host environment alter their output to match the host environment and produce upper-layer neurons (Desai and McConnell, 2000; McConnell, 1988; McConnell and Kaznowski, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to classic transplantation experiments.

claim: The adult Drosophila central brain is built from ~100 neuroblasts.
source: The adult Drosophila central brain is built from ~100 neuroblasts (Lee et al., 2020; Urbach and Technau, 2004; Wong et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013a) that divide continuously from L1 to L3 (Homem et al., 2014; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Central brain neuroblasts divide continuously from L1 to L3.
source: The adult Drosophila central brain is built from ~100 neuroblasts (Lee et al., 2020; Urbach and Technau, 2004; Wong et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013a) that divide continuously from L1 to L3 (Homem et al., 2014; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each asymmetric division of a neuroblast regenerates the neuroblast and produces an intermediate progenitor called ganglion mother cell (GMC) that divides only once, typically producing two different cell types.
source: Each asymmetric division regenerates the neuroblast and produces an intermediate progenitor called ganglion mother cell (GMC) that divides only once, typically producing two different cell types (Lin et al., 2010; Spana and Doe, 1996; Truman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During larval life central brain neuroblasts divide 50–60 times, sequentially producing many different neuronal types.
source: Thus, during larval life central brain neuroblasts divide 50–60 times, sequentially producing many different neuronal types.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge about neuroblast divisions.

claim: All central brain neuroblasts progress through opposing temporal gradients of two RNA-binding proteins as they age: IGF-II mRNA binding protein (Imp) when they are young and Syncrip (Syp) when they are old.
source: All central brain neuroblasts progress through opposing temporal gradients of two RNA-binding proteins as they age: IGF-II mRNA binding protein (Imp) when they are young and Syncrip (Syp) when they are old (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017b; Syed et al., 2017a; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of Imp or Syp in antennal lobe or Type II neuroblasts affects the ratio of young to old neuronal types.
source: Loss of Imp or Syp in antennal lobe or Type II neuroblasts affects the ratio of young to old neuronal types (Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Imp and Syp affect neuroblast lifespan.
source: Imp and Syp also affect neuroblast lifespan (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A single temporal program can affect both the diversity of neuronal types produced and their numbers.
source: Thus, a single temporal program can affect both the diversity of neuronal types produced and their numbers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion drawn from the effects of Imp and Syp on neuroblast function.

claim: Ecdysone triggers all the major developmental transitions including progression into the different larval stages and entry in pupation.
source: Ecdysone triggers all the major developmental transitions including progression into the different larval stages and entry in pupation (Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The majority of central brain neuroblasts are not responsive to ecdysone until mid-larval life when they begin to express the Ecdysone Receptor (EcR).
source: The majority of central brain neuroblasts are not responsive to ecdysone until mid-larval life when they begin to express the Ecdysone Receptor (EcR) (Syed et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expressing a dominant-negative version of EcR (EcR-DN) in Type II neuroblasts delays the Imp to Syp transition that normally occurs ~60 hr after larval hatching (ALH).
source: Expressing a dominant-negative version of EcR (EcR-DN) in Type II neuroblasts delays the Imp to Syp transition that normally occurs ~60 hr after larval hatching (ALH).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous work.

claim: The mushroom body is comprised of ~2000 neurons (Kenyon cells) that belong to only three main neuronal types that have unique morphologies and play distinct roles in learning and memory.
source: The mushroom body is comprised of ~2000 neurons (Kenyon cells) that belong to only three main neuronal types that have unique morphologies and play distinct roles in learning and memory (Cognigni et al., 2018; Ito et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mushroom body neurons receive input mainly from ~200 projection neurons that each relays odor information from olfactory receptor neurons.
source: They receive input mainly from ~200 projection neurons that each relays odor information from olfactory receptor neurons (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Each projection neuron connects to a random subset of Kenyon cells and each Kenyon cell receives input from ~7 different projection neurons.
source: Each projection neuron connects to a random subset of Kenyon cells and each Kenyon cell receives input from ~7 different projection neurons (Jefferis et al., 2007; Murthy et al., 2008; Turner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The connectivity pattern of mushroom body neurons requires a large number of mushroom body neurons (~2,000) to represent complex odors.
source: This connectivity pattern requires a large number of mushroom body neurons (~2,000) to represent complex odors (Hige, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mushroom body neurons are born from four identical neuroblasts that divide continuously from the late embryonic stages until the end of pupation (~9 days for ~250 divisions each).
source: Mushroom body neurons are born from four identical neuroblasts that divide continuously (unlike any other neuroblast) from the late embryonic stages until the end of pupation (~9 days for ~250 divisions each) (Figure 1A; Ito et al., 1997; Kraft et al., 2016; Kunz et al., 2012; Kurusu et al., 2009; Lee et al., 1999; Pahl et al., 2019; Siegrist et al., 2010; Sipe and Siegrist, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to Figure 1A and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The two neurons born from each mushroom body GMC are identical.
source: Furthermore, the two neurons born from each mushroom body GMC are identical.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a unique feature of mushroom body development.

claim: The neuronal simplicity of the adult mushroom body makes it ideal to study how extrinsic cues might affect diversity since the loss of any single neuronal type is obvious given that each is represented hundreds of times.
source: The neuronal simplicity of the adult mushroom body makes it ideal to study how extrinsic cues might affect diversity since the loss of any single neuronal type is obvious given that each is represented hundreds of times.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for using the mushroom body as a model system.

claim: During early larval stages, mushroom body neuroblasts express high levels of Imp and Chinmo in neurons to specify γ identity for ~85 neuroblast divisions.
source: During early larval stages, mushroom body neuroblasts express high levels of Imp (red) and Chinmo (red) in neurons to specify γ identity for ~85 neuroblast divisions (red-dashed box).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: From mid-L3 to metamorphosis, when Imp and Syp are both at low levels, the mushroom body neuroblast divides ~40 times to produce α'β' neurons.
source: From mid-L3 to metamorphosis, when Imp and Syp (cyan) are both at low levels, the same neuroblast divides ~40 times to produce α'β' neurons (magenta-dashed box).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Low Chinmo regulates the expression of Mamo, a terminal selector of α'β' identity.
source: Low Chinmo regulates the expression Mamo, a terminal selector of α'β' identity.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: From the beginning of metamorphosis throughout pupal development, high Syp leads to αβ neurons.
source: From the beginning of metamorphosis throughout pupal development, high Syp leads to αβ neurons (cyan-dashed outline).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: The first-born γ neurons remodel during development to project into a single, medial lobe in the adult.
source: The first-born γ neurons (red) remodel during development to project into a single, medial lobe in the adult. This lobe is the most anterior of the medial lobes.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Axons from α'β' neurons bifurcate to project into the vertical and medial α' and β' lobes.
source: Axons from α'β' neurons (magenta) bifurcate to project into the vertical and medial α' and β' lobes. The β' lobe is posterior to the γ lobe.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: The last-born αβ neurons bifurcate their axons into the vertical projecting α lobe and medial projecting β lobe.
source: The last-born αβ neurons (cyan) also bifurcate their axons into the vertical projecting α lobe and medial projecting β lobe. The α lobe is positioned adjacent and medial to the α' lobe. The β lobe is the most posterior medial lobe.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: In wildtype clones induced at L1, GFP+ axons project to all five mushroom body lobes: α, α΄, β, β' and γ.
source: In wildtype clones induced at L1, GFP+ axons projected to all five mushroom body lobes: α, α΄, β, β' (hidden behind the γ lobe in max projections), and γ (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In clones mutant for babo, GFP+ axons are not detected within the α'β' lobes.
source: In clones mutant for babo, we did not detect GFP+ axons within the α'β' lobes, which remained visible by Trio staining due to the presence of wildtype α'β' neurons (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: γ neurons within babo mutant clones remain unpruned.
source: In addition, and as previously described, γ neurons within babo mutant clones remained unpruned (visualized by vertical GFP+ axons that were Trio+ and FasII+), providing a positive control since γ remodeling is known to require activin signaling (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Awasaki et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2013b; Zheng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E, with citations to previous literature.

claim: Babo is the sole Type I receptor in the activin pathway.
source: Babo is the sole Type I receptor in the activin pathway (a member of the TGFβ family of signaling molecules).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: Babo acts through the transcription factor Smad on X (Smad2).
source: Babo with its Type II co-receptors binds four different activin ligands and acts through the transcription factor Smad on X (Smad2) (Brummel et al., 1999; Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Smad2 mutant clones are missing α'β' neurons and contain unpruned γ neurons.
source: Similar to babo mutant clones, Smad2 clones were missing α'β' neurons and also contained unpruned γ neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Strong Trio and Mamo label α'β' neuron cell bodies in the adult.
source: Using antibodies against Trio and Mamo that strongly label α'β' neuron cell bodies in the adult (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J; Alyagor et al., 2018; Awasaki et al., 2000; Croset et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), we detected strong Trio+ and Mamo+ cells within adult GFP+ clones induced at L1 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous literature and shown in figures.

claim: In babo mutant clones, the vast majority of strong Trio+ and Mamo+ cells inside clones are missing compared to surrounding wildtype neurons.
source: In babo mutant clones however, the vast majority of strong Trio+ and Mamo+ cells inside clones were missing compared to surrounding wildtype neurons (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1L), suggesting that α'β' neurons were not specified.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In wildtype MARCM clones affecting a single mushroom body neuroblast, the percentage of all α'β' neurons that were present within the clones was 25.5 ± 0.7%.
source: In wildtype MARCM clones affecting a single mushroom body neuroblast (n = 7), the percentage of all α'β' neurons that were present within the clones was 25.5 ± 0.7%, the expected ratio since each mushroom body is built from four identical neuroblasts (Figure 1H; Ito et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In babo mutant clones, the percentage of α'β' neurons within clones was 2.2 ± 0.4%.
source: In comparison, in babo mutant clones (n = 8) the percentage of α'β' neurons within clones was 2.2 ± 0.4% (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There is no significant difference in average clone sizes between wildtype and babo mutant clones labeled with mb-Gal4.
source: We next sought to determine the fate of the missing α'β' neurons in babo clones, particularly since there was no significant difference in average clone sizes between mutant and control clones labeled with mb-Gal4 (wildtype: clone size = 533.6 ± 33.3, n = 7; babo: clone size = 551.3 ± 17.6, n = 7) (Figure 1H'), which suggests that there is no defect in neuroblast proliferation, and that α'β' neurons are not lost by cell death in babo clones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H'.

claim: α'β' neurons are not lost by cell death in babo clones.
source: However, to directly test whether cell death played a role, we expressed the caspase inhibitor P35 in babo mutant clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). However, α'β' neurons were still missing in the adult (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating that α'β' neurons are not generated and then die.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The average number of γ neurons trended higher in babo mutant clones, although not significantly.
source: Using R71G10-Gal4 (Issman-Zecharya and Schuldiner, 2014) (referred to as γ-Gal4), the average number of γ neurons trended higher in babo mutant clones, although not significantly (wildtype: 154.3 ± 11.4, n = 10; babo: 178.4 ± 11.9, n = 12) (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E), likely because the number of γ neurons directly depends on the time of clone induction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: α'β' neurons, marked by R41C07-Gal4, were mostly missing in babo mutant clones compared to wildtype clones.
source: α'β' neurons, marked by R41C07-Gal4 (referred to as α'β'-Gal4), were mostly missing in babo mutant clones compared to wildtype clones (wildtype: 81.5 ± 3.6, n = 4; babo: 2.1 ± 0.5, n = 8,) consistent with our previous results when counting strong Mamo+ cells in babo clones marked by mb-Gal4 (Figure 1H, Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The average number of αβ neurons, marked by R44E04-Gal4, was significantly reduced in babo versus wildtype clones.
source: The average number of αβ neurons, marked by R44E04-Gal4 (referred to as αβ-Gal4), was significantly reduced in babo versus wildtype clones (wildtype: 276 ± 9.1, n = 7,; babo: 228.9 ± 13.2, n = 8) (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J–M).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Additional γ neurons are likely produced in babo mutant clones.
source: Together, these results suggest that additional γ neurons are likely produced, and that fewer αβ neurons are generated, in babo mutant clones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data showing trends in neuronal numbers.

claim: Fewer αβ neurons are generated in babo mutant clones.
source: Together, these results suggest that additional γ neurons are likely produced, and that fewer αβ neurons are generated, in babo mutant clones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the quantification data.

claim: babo is expressed evenly through time in mushroom body neuroblasts.
source: Based on published transcriptome data collected from mushroom body neuroblasts at different developmental stages (Liu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016), babo is expressed evenly through time in mushroom body neuroblasts, unlike the two RNA binding proteins Imp and Syp (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, based on published transcriptome data.

claim: The average Imp to Syp ratio was significantly higher in babo neuroblasts compared to wildtype neuroblasts at L3.
source: The average Imp to Syp ratio was significantly higher in babo neuroblasts (ratio: 4.2 ± 0.4; n = 9 from 4 different brains) compared to wildtype neuroblasts (ratio: 2.4 ± 0.2; n = 23 from the same 4 brains as babo) at L3, driven by a significantly higher Imp level in mutant neuroblasts (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) while Syp was not significantly different (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The α'β' neuronal marker Mamo was lost in babo mutant clones at L3.
source: In addition, the α'β' neuronal marker Mamo (Liu et al., 2019) was lost in babo mutant clones at L3 while the level of Chinmo was higher in these neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C'''), consistent with the notion that high Imp levels block α'β' specification through maintained higher levels of Chinmo that likely lead to the increased production of γ neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C'''.

claim: The level of Chinmo was higher in babo mutant neurons at L3.
source: In addition, the α'β' neuronal marker Mamo (Liu et al., 2019) was lost in babo mutant clones at L3 while the level of Chinmo was higher in these neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C'''), consistent with the notion that high Imp levels block α'β' specification through maintained higher levels of Chinmo that likely lead to the increased production of γ neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C'''.

claim: The significantly higher Imp to Syp ratio in babo mutant neuroblasts persisted even ~24 hr After Pupal Formation (APF).
source: The significantly higher Imp to Syp ratio in babo mutant neuroblasts persisted even ~24 hr After Pupal Formation (APF) (babo ratio: 0.58 ± 0.11; n = 7 from 6 different brains; wildtype ratio: 0.27 ±. 02; n = 27 from the same 6 brains as babo), once again driven by higher Imp levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I.

claim: Activin signaling lowers Imp levels at late larval and early pupal stages.
source: Together, these results indicate that activin signaling lowers Imp levels at late larval and early pupal stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data showing higher Imp levels in babo mutant neuroblasts.

claim: Although Imp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts and persisted longer, the absolute level of Imp still decreased significantly albeit with prolonged kinetics.
source: Importantly, although Imp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts and persisted longer, the absolute level of Imp still decreased significantly albeit with prolonged kinetics, while the absolute level of Syp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts at ~24 hr APF vs. L3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–J'): Thus, these changes are either intrinsically regulated or are affected by additional extrinsic factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–J'.

claim: The absolute level of Syp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts at ~24 hr APF vs. L3.
source: Importantly, although Imp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts and persisted longer, the absolute level of Imp still decreased significantly albeit with prolonged kinetics, while the absolute level of Syp was higher in babo mutant neuroblasts at ~24 hr APF vs. L3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–J'): Thus, these changes are either intrinsically regulated or are affected by additional extrinsic factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–J'.

claim: The lack of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones even though Imp levels were finally low at ~24 hr APF suggests that α'β' specification may only occur from L3 to the start of pupation.
source: Our finding that Imp and Chinmo were higher in babo mutant neuroblasts and neurons at L3 is also consistent with our suggestion that additional γ neurons are produced during the α'β' time window. The lack of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones even though Imp levels were finally low at ~24 hr APF suggests that α'β' specification may only occur from L3 to the start of pupation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the temporal expression data.

claim: Activin signaling acts in mushroom body neuroblasts, and not in neurons, to specify the α'β' fate.
source: These results show that activin signaling acts in mushroom body neuroblasts, and not in neurons, to specify the α'β' fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from GMC clone experiments.

claim: α'β' neurons were present in babo GMC clones induced during mid-late L3.
source: To test if activin signaling functions post-mitotically in prospective α'β' neurons, we characterized the morphology of babo mutant neurons born from ganglion mother cell (GMC) clones induced during mid-late L3, the time at which α'β' neurons are born. GMCs are intermediate progenitors that divide only once to produce two neurons. In this way, the role of Babo in prospective α'β' neurons can be tested without affecting mushroom body neuroblasts: α'β' neurons were present in babo GMC clones (n = 34/34), observable by axonal projections into the Trio labeled α'β' lobes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–K').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–K'.

claim: In the majority of babo GMC clones induced at L1, γ axons remained unpruned.
source: As a positive control for the efficiency of babo GMC clones, we also made babo GMC clones at L1 to target γ neurons. In the majority of cases, γ axons remained unpruned (n = 8/10, Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–L'; Zheng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–L'.

claim: Expressing a constitutively active form of the Babo receptor (UAS-Babo-Act) throughout development in MARCM clones significantly increased the number of α'β' neurons.
source: We expressed a constitutively active form of the Babo receptor (UAS-Babo-Act) throughout development in MARCM clones with mb-Gal4 and assessed the total number of α'β' neurons in the adult by strong Mamo expression. While in wildtype clones the percentage of α'β' neurons was 25.5 ± 0.7% (n = 7), the number of α'β' neurons present within UAS-Babo-Act clones significantly increased to 32 ± 1.4% (n = 4) (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: Mamo was expressed in neurons in UAS-Babo-Act clones at early L3, when γ neurons are normally being produced.
source: To ask when these additional α'β' neurons were produced, we characterized the expression of the α'β' marker Mamo in young neurons at early L3, when γ neurons are being produced. In comparison to adjacent wildtype neurons, Mamo was expressed in neurons in UAS-Babo-Act clones at this stage (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: Constitutively expressing an activated version of Babo did not result in adult clones consisting entirely of α'β' neurons.
source: Importantly, constitutively expressing an activated version of Babo did not result in adult clones consisting entirely of α'β' neurons, highlighting that activin signaling alone is not master regulator of the α'β' fate and that other components are necessary to specify this neuronal type.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the UAS-Babo-Act experiments.

claim: Glia secrete the activin ligand Myoglianin (Myo) to initiate γ neuron remodeling by activating EcR at L3.
source: Glia secrete the activin ligand Myoglianin (Myo) to initiate γ neuron remodeling by activating EcR at L3 (Awasaki et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Knocking-down myo by expressing UAS-myo-RNAi with repo-Gal4 dramatically reduced the number of α'β' neurons.
source: To test this, we knocked-down myo by expressing UAS-myo-RNAi with repo-Gal4, a driver expressed in all glia, and quantified the total number of α'β' neurons based on strong Mamo expression in the adult (Figure 4A–E). In comparison to control (428.9 ± 16.2, n = 10), the number of α'β' neurons was dramatically reduced (106.6 ± 11.4; n = 10) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: Mamo was not expressed in mushroom body neurons at L3 when myo was knocked down in glia.
source: Mamo was also not expressed in mushroom body neurons at L3 (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F–G.

claim: EcR was not expressed in γ neurons at L3 when myo was knocked down in glia.
source: Importantly, EcR was not expressed in γ neurons at this stage, providing a positive control for the efficiency of UAS-myo-RNAi (Awasaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a positive control for the myo knockdown experiment.

claim: Low Imp levels are required at L3 for α'β' specification.
source: We therefore characterized Mamo expression in young neurons at L3 following knockdown (UAS-Imp-RNAi) or overexpression (UAS-Imp-OE) of Imp with mb-Gal4. (Figure 5A–C; Liu et al., 2015). Consistent with our model, Mamo was not expressed in either condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Knocking-down Syp by expressing UAS-Syp-RNAi led to the loss of Mamo.
source: In comparison, although knocking-down Syp by expressing UAS-Syp-RNAi led to the loss of Mamo, its early overexpression (UAS-Syp-OE) did not (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D–E.

claim: Early overexpression of Syp (UAS-Syp-OE) did not affect Mamo expression.
source: In comparison, although knocking-down Syp by expressing UAS-Syp-RNAi led to the loss of Mamo, its early overexpression (UAS-Syp-OE) did not (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D–E.

claim: Low Imp and low or high Syp levels are required for α'β' specification.
source: We conclude that low Imp and low or high Syp levels are required for α'β' specification.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the Imp and Syp manipulation experiments.

claim: Expressing UAS-babo rescued the loss of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones.
source: However, we could rescue babo mutant clones by expressing UAS-babo (21.1 ± 2.4%, n = 6) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1K–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H, K–M, P.

claim: Overexpressing Syp (UAS-Syp-OE) did not rescue α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones.
source: Overexpressing Syp (UAS-Syp-OE) to reduce the altered Imp:Syp ratio in babo mutant clones also did not rescue α'β' neurons (1.8 ± 0.5%, n = 7) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1O–P), further highlighting that Imp but not Syp levels are important for α'β' specification.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J, O–P.

claim: Expressing UAS-EcR-DN driven by mb-Gal4 led to the loss of GFP+ mutant axons within adult α'β' lobes.
source: We confirmed these results by also expressing UAS-EcR-DN driven by mb-Gal4 and were unable to detect GFP+ mutant axons within adult α'β' lobes marked by Trio (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Strong Trio+ and Mamo+ cells were missing inside UAS-EcR-DN mutant clones compared to wildtype clones.
source: In addition, strong Trio+ and Mamo+ cells were missing inside UAS-EcR-DN mutant clones compared to wildtype clones (wildtype: 25.5 ± 0.7%, n = 7; UAS-EcR-DN: 3.4 ± 0.6%, n = 6) (Figure 6C–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: α'β' neurons were still present in mutant clones for the EcR co-receptor ultraspiracle (usp).
source: However, we were surprised to find that α'β' neurons were still present in mutant clones for the EcR co-receptor ultraspiracle (usp) (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the average Imp to Syp protein ratio at L3 in UAS-EcR-DN expressing mushroom body neuroblasts with mb-Gal4.
source: First, unlike our result in babo mutant neuroblasts, we did not observe a significant difference in the average Imp to Syp protein ratio at L3 in UAS-EcR-DN expressing mushroom body neuroblasts with mb-Gal4 (UAS-EcR-DN ratio: 2.6 ± 0.7, n = 4 from four different brains; wildtype ratio: 1.7 ± 0.3, n = 27 from the same four brains as UAS-EcR-DN) (Figure 6G–J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–D').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6G–J.

claim: Driving even stronger expression of UAS-EcR-DN in mushroom body neuroblasts with NB-Gal4 and labeling all adult neurons with mb2-Gal4 did not lead to the loss of α'β' neurons in the adult.
source: Driving even stronger expression of UAS-EcR-DN in mushroom body neuroblasts with inscuteable-Gal4 (referred to as NB-Gal4) and labeling all adult neurons with R13F02-Gal4 (referred to as mb2-Gal4) (Jenett et al., 2012) also did not lead to the loss of α'β' neurons in the adult (Figure 6K–N, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6K–N.

claim: EcR-DN only blocks α'β' specification when expressed in newborn mushroom body neurons, not in neuroblasts.
source: These results indicate that EcR-DN only blocks α'β' specification when expressed in newborn mushroom body neurons, not in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments using different Gal4 drivers.

claim: Mamo expression was lost in UAS-EcR-DN expressing clones driven by mb-Gal4.
source: Given these results, we next asked whether expressing UAS-EcR-DN affects Mamo during development, which labels newborn postmitotic α'β' neurons (Liu et al., 2019); Mamo expression was lost in UAS-EcR-DN expressing clones driven by mb-Gal4 (Figure 6P) but it was not affected by the expression of UAS-EcR-RNAi (Figure 6Q), although the RNAi was effective since we could not detect EcR protein in mushroom body neurons (Figure 6O, Figure 6Q).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6P.

claim: Mamo expression was not affected by the expression of UAS-EcR-RNAi.
source: Given these results, we next asked whether expressing UAS-EcR-DN affects Mamo during development, which labels newborn postmitotic α'β' neurons (Liu et al., 2019); Mamo expression was lost in UAS-EcR-DN expressing clones driven by mb-Gal4 (Figure 6P) but it was not affected by the expression of UAS-EcR-RNAi (Figure 6Q), although the RNAi was effective since we could not detect EcR protein in mushroom body neurons (Figure 6O, Figure 6Q).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6Q.

claim: Mamo and EcR were mutually exclusive at L3.
source: Given these contradictory results, we compared Mamo and EcR expression at L3. However, Mamo and EcR were mutually exclusive as EcR was not expressed in newborn α'β' neurons (see Figure 6O''), which precludes the possibility that EcR-DN inhibits EcR function in these neurons and might therefore act through off-target inhibition of Mamo.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6O''.

claim: EcR protein was not detected in mushroom body neuroblasts and young neurons at wandering L3.
source: These results confirm the lack of EcR protein in mushroom body neuroblasts and young neurons at wandering L3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H), although EcR was clearly expressed in mature (mostly γ) neurons at this stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–H''; Lee et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2015; Marchetti and Tavosanis, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: Expressing UAS-EcR-B1 did not rescue the loss of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones.
source: Finally, we were unable to rescue the loss of α'β' neurons in babo mutant clones by expressing UAS-EcR-B1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J), consistent with the notion that EcR does not function in α'β' specification downstream of activin signaling (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: It is unlikely that ecdysone signaling is involved in α'β' specification although it might still be used later during α'β' differentiation.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that ecdysone signaling is involved in α'β' specification although it might still be used later during α'β' differentiation (Marchetti and Tavosanis, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the ecdysone signaling experiments.

claim: The loss of α'β' neurons when expressing UAS-EcR-DN is caused by artifactual inhibition of Mamo.
source: We conclude that the loss of α'β' neurons when expressing UAS-EcR-DN is caused by artifactual inhibition of Mamo (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the EcR experiments.

claim: At the end of the γ temporal window (mid-L3), activin signaling from glia acts to rapidly reduce Imp levels in mushroom body neuroblasts without significantly affecting Syp.
source: However, at the end of the γ temporal window (mid-L3), activin signaling from glia acts to rapidly reduce Imp levels in mushroom body neuroblasts without significantly affecting Syp, establishing a period of low Imp (and thus low Chinmo in neurons) and also low Syp.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Low Chinmo regulates the expression in neurons of mamo, whose mRNA is stabilized by Syp.
source: Low Chinmo then regulates the expression in neurons of maternal gene required for meiosis (mamo), which encodes a transcription factor that specifies the α'β' fate and whose mRNA is stabilized by Syp (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The production of αβ identity begins when Imp is further decreased and Syp levels are high during pupation.
source: The production of αβ identity begins when Imp is further decreased and Syp levels are high during pupation (modeled in Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Low Chinmo in αβ neurons is partly regulated by ecdysone signaling through the activation of Let-7-C, which targets chinmo for degradation.
source: Low Chinmo in αβ neurons is also partly regulated by ecdysone signaling through the activation of Let-7-C, which targets chinmo for degradation (Kucherenko et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pioneer-αβ neurons are the first of the αβ class to be specified when Imp is still present at very low levels during pupation.
source: We believe that there is both an increase in the number of γ neurons and of the pioneer-αβ neuron subclass because pioneer-αβ neurons are the first of the αβ class to be specified (when Imp is still present at very low levels) during pupation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the observed phenotypes.

claim: At least seven subtypes of mushroom body neurons exist: 2 γ, 2 α'β' and 3 αβ.
source: In this study, we have focused on the three main classes of mushroom body neurons although at least seven subtypes exist: 2 γ, 2 α'β' and 3 αβ (Aso et al., 2014; Shih et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The subtypes of mushroom body neurons are specified sequentially.
source: The subtypes are specified sequentially (Aso et al., 2014) suggesting that each of the three broad mushroom body temporal windows can be subdivided further, either by fine-scale reading of the changing Imp and Syp gradients, by additional extrinsic cues, or perhaps by a tTF series as in other neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activin signaling times the Imp to Syp transition for mushroom body neuroblasts, similar to the function of ecdysone for other central brain neuroblasts.
source: We have also shown that activin signaling times the Imp to Syp transition for mushroom body neuroblasts, similar to the function of ecdysone for other central brain neuroblasts (Syed et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In both activin and ecdysone signaling cases, the Imp to Syp switch still occurs, indicating that a separate independent clock continues to tick.
source: In both cases however, the switch still occurs, indicating that a separate independent clock continues to tick.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Hindbrain neural stem cells progressively produce motor neurons followed by serotonergic neurons before switching to producing glia.
source: For example, hindbrain neural stem cells progressively produce motor neurons followed by serotonergic neurons before switching to producing glia (Chleilat et al., 2018; Dias et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The motor neuron to serotonergic neuron switch in hindbrain neural stem cells is fine-tuned by TGFβ signaling.
source: The motor neuron to serotonergic neuron switch is fine-tuned by TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an example of extrinsic cue function in vertebrate neurogenesis.

claim: The specification of α'β' neurons begins at mid-L3 with the onset of Mamo expression.
source: The specification of α'β' neurons begins at mid-L3 with the onset of Mamo expression (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: High levels of EcR are detected in mature mushroom body neurons starting at late L3.
source: In contrast, high levels of EcR are detected in mature mushroom body neurons starting at late L3 (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mamo expression precedes EcR expression in mushroom body neurons.
source: Thus, Mamo expression precedes EcR expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the temporal expression patterns.

claim: The non-overlapping expression patterns of Mamo and EcR suggest that ecdysone signaling does not regulate Mamo and therefore cannot control the specification of α'β' neurons.
source: These non-overlapping expression patterns suggest that ecdysone signaling does not regulate Mamo and therefore cannot control the specification of α'β' neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the expression data.

claim: Ecdysone might function later during α'β' differentiation, particularly during pupation when all mushroom body neurons express EcR.
source: Nevertheless, ecdysone might still function later during α'β' differentiation, particularly during pupation when all mushroom body neurons express EcR.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about potential later roles of ecdysone.

claim: EcR must be first expressed in the target cells of interest in order to make conclusions about ecdysone function using UAS-EcR-DN.
source: However, EcR must be first be expressed in the target cells of interest in order to make any conclusions about ecdysone function using UAS-EcR-DN.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a methodological consideration.

claim: Subdividing the broad Imp and Syp temporal windows by extrinsic cues may be a simple way to increase neuronal diversity in other central brain neuroblasts.
source: We propose that subdividing the broad Imp and Syp temporal windows by extrinsic cues may be a simple way to increase neuronal diversity in other central brain neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Mechanisms of intrinsic temporal patterning are conserved between Drosophila and vertebrates.
source: Mechanisms of intrinsic temporal patterning are also conserved (Alsiö et al., 2013; Elliott et al., 2008; Holguera and Desplan, 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2015; Mattar et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vertebrate retinal progenitor cells use an intrinsic tTF cascade to bias young, middle, and old retinal fates.
source: For example, vertebrate retinal progenitor cells use an intrinsic tTF cascade to bias young, middle, and old retinal fates (Elliott et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2020; Mattar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two of the factors (Ikaros and Casz1) used for intrinsic temporal patterning in vertebrate retinal progenitors are orthologs to the Drosophila tTFs Hb and Cas.
source: Two of the factors (Ikaros and Casz1) used for intrinsic temporal patterning are orthologs to the Drosophila tTFs Hb and Cas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as evidence for conservation of temporal patterning mechanisms.
